name: Rara & the Far West
tagline: Tigers, Rara Lake and the road to Kailash
meta_description: Far West Nepal tours: Bardia tiger safaris, Rara Lake by flight or trek, Khaptad, Shuklaphanta, Limi Valley and Simikot. Prices, seasons and permits.
summary: Nepal's far west runs from the Terai parks of Bardia and Shuklaphanta, where 162 tigers were counted in 2026, up to Rara Lake at about 2,990 m and roadless Humla on the Tibet border. Fly to Nepalgunj or Dhangadhi, visit the parks from October to April and the hills April–June or late September–November.
intro: West of Lumbini, Nepal changes pace. Tourist numbers fall away, hotels thin out and the country opens into some of its least visited land: the Terai grasslands of Bardia and Shuklaphanta on the Indian border, the pine-covered hills of Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces, and Humla, the roadless district that touches Tibet. Nepalgunj, at 150 m and 6 km from the Rupaidiha border, is the hub. Almost every trip here starts with an hour's flight from Kathmandu to Nepalgunj or Dhangadhi, or a drive across the border from Lucknow.

Bardia National Park, 968 km² of sal forest and grassland on the Karnali river, is the reason most visitors come. Nepal's 2026 census counted 112 tigers there, and the park's full-day jeep and walking safaris, run from the Tharu village of Thakurdwara, give patient guests a real chance of seeing one without a queue of vehicles. Further west, Shuklaphanta holds 50 tigers and Nepal's largest herd of swamp deer on open phanta grassland. Both parks are at their best from February to April, when the grass has been cut and the water shrinks.

In the hills, Rara Lake is the headline. Nepal's largest lake, 10.8 km² at about 2,990 m, sits in a ring of blue pine in Mugu district and is reached by a 45-minute flight from Nepalgunj to Talcha or a 5–6 day trek from Jumla over passes near 3,600 m. Khaptad National Park, a plateau of meadows at about 3,000 m, and the small lakes of Ramaroshan offer quieter walks from the Dhangadhi side, with views of Api and Saipal on the skyline.

Humla is the far end of the map. Simikot, its headquarters at 2,910 m, has no road link to the south and is reached by small plane from Nepalgunj. Kailash pilgrims pass through on the helicopter route to Hilsa, and trekkers continue up the Karnali to the Tibetan Buddhist villages of the Limi Valley, crossing Nyalu La at about 4,950 m. Lodges here are basic, flights depend on the weather and treks need permits and full camping support, which our packages arrange.

highlights.title: Tiger safaris on foot in Bardia
highlights.text: Bardia's naturalists lead full-day walking and jeep safaris from Thakurdwara, waiting at river crossings on the Geruwa channel of the Karnali where tigers come to drink. With 112 tigers counted in 2026 and few other vehicles in the park, three or four nights between February and May give guests a fair chance of a sighting.

highlights.title: Rara Lake, Nepal's largest
highlights.text: Rara covers 10.8 km² at about 2,990 m and reaches 167 m deep. A 13 km path circles the shore through blue pine and spruce, and Murma Top above the lake looks over the whole basin to the Kanjiroba and Saipal ranges. Fly to Talcha in 45 minutes from Nepalgunj or trek in from Jumla.

highlights.title: Swamp deer of Shuklaphanta
highlights.text: The open phanta grassland of Shuklaphanta, 305 km² beside the Mahakali river, holds Nepal's largest herd of swamp deer, often grazing in groups of hundreds on winter mornings. Tigers, wild elephants and the endangered Bengal florican share the grassland. The park is about 1.5 hours by road from Dhangadhi airport.

highlights.title: Khaptad's high meadows
highlights.text: Khaptad National Park is a rolling plateau at about 3,000–3,300 m where four districts meet, with open meadows called patans, oak and rhododendron forest and the ashram of the hermit Khaptad Baba. It takes a two-day walk from the roadhead at Jhingrana, and clear mornings show Api and Saipal to the north.

highlights.title: Into the Limi Valley
highlights.text: Limi's three Tibetan Buddhist villages, Til, Halji and Jang, lie between about 3,660 and 4,100 m close to the Tibet border, and Halji's Rinchenling Gompa is centuries old. Our 19-day camping trek from Simikot crosses Nara La and Nyalu La at about 4,950 m, with blue sheep and kiang on the high pastures.

highlights.title: Simikot, gateway to Kailash
highlights.text: Simikot, at 2,910 m, is the shortest way from Nepal to Mount Kailash. Pilgrims fly Nepalgunj–Simikot in 40–50 minutes, then take a 20–30 minute helicopter hop to Hilsa on the border and drive on through Purang. The town itself has no road to the south and runs on small planes, mules and porters.

getting_there: Nepalgunj is the hub for most of the region. Buddha Air and Shree Airlines fly Kathmandu–Nepalgunj in about an hour, and small planes leave Nepalgunj in the morning for Talcha (Rara, 45 min), Jumla (40 min) and Simikot (40–50 min), weather permitting. Bardia's lodges at Thakurdwara are about 95 km, or 2.5–3 hours, by road from Nepalgunj. For the western end, fly Kathmandu–Dhangadhi in about 1 h 15 min, then drive 1.5 hours to Shuklaphanta or a long day into the hills for Khaptad and Ramaroshan. From India, the Rupaidiha–Nepalgunj border is about 190 km, or 4–5 hours, from Lucknow, and the Gauriphanta and Banbasa crossings lead to Dhangadhi and Mahendranagar. By road from Kathmandu, Nepalgunj is 12–14 hours away.
permits: Bardia and Shuklaphanta charge a daily park entry fee, which has been NPR 1,500 plus VAT for foreigners and NPR 750 for SAARC nationals, including Indians. Rara and Khaptad national parks have charged NPR 3,000 for foreigners and NPR 1,500 for SAARC nationals. Hill trekkers need a TIMS card and, under current rules, a licensed guide. Upper Humla, including the Karnali trail to Hilsa and the Limi Valley, is a restricted area: the permit has cost US$50 per person for the first seven days and US$10 per day after, issued through a registered agency. Check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Bardia 8 to 23 °C, foggy mornings; Rara −10 to 5 °C with snow
months.summary: January suits the Terai only. Bardia and Shuklaphanta are cool and often foggy until about 10 am, then sunny, which makes for comfortable full-day safaris, though tall grass still hides tigers. Tharu villages around Bardia and Dhangadhi celebrate Maghi in mid-month with feasts, dances and family visits. In the hills Rara Lake freezes at the edges, snow lies in Jumla and Simikot, and many flights to the mountain airstrips are cancelled. Treks in Humla and Khaptad are closed in practice.
months.tip: Bring a fleece and windproof jacket for open-jeep safaris, because foggy mornings in Bardia feel close to 8 °C.

months.weather: Bardia 10 to 26 °C, dry with clear afternoons; Jumla −5 to 12 °C
months.summary: February opens the best tiger season. From late January park staff cut and burn the tall grass in Bardia and Shuklaphanta, so animals become easier to see, and days are warm without the heat of April. Swamp deer herds gather on Shuklaphanta's open phanta. Nepalgunj is pleasant for a night stop, with cool evenings for the bazaar and Bageshwari Temple. The hills are still cold: Rara and Khaptad lie under snow and flights to Talcha and Simikot remain irregular.
months.tip: Book Bardia lodges early for February and March, because the small lodges in Thakurdwara fill with wildlife photographers.

months.summary: March brings warm, dry days to the Terai and the first good walking weather in the middle hills. Bardia and Shuklaphanta are excellent for tigers, rhinos and elephants as water sources shrink. Rhododendrons flower around Ramaroshan and on the lower slopes of Khaptad, and the lakes at Ramaroshan make a gentle 3–4 day trip from the Dhangadhi side. Higher up, Rara still has snow in shaded forest, and Jumla flights become steadier towards the end of the month.
months.tip: Pair a Bardia safari with Shuklaphanta in March; the 250 km drive between them takes 5–6 hours on the East–West Highway.

months.weather: Rara 0 to 15 °C; Bardia 20 to 37 °C, hot and dry
months.summary: April is the one month when both halves of the region work well. In Bardia, tigers come to the last pools and river channels, and sightings peak despite midday heat near 37 °C. In the hills, flights to Talcha and Jumla settle into a regular pattern, the trek from Jumla to Rara opens, and Khaptad's meadows dry out. The Nepali New Year in mid-April brings domestic visitors to Rara, so lodges fill. Limi and the high Humla passes are still snowbound.
months.tip: Start safaris at dawn in April and rest at a shaded watchpoint from 11 am to 3 pm.

months.weather: Rara 4 to 19 °C, mostly dry; Nepalgunj 25 to 40 °C
months.summary: May is the peak month for Rara Lake and the hill treks. Days at the lake are mild, the water is calm and blue, and the Jumla–Rara trail is dry. Khaptad and Ramaroshan are green and pleasant. The Terai is very hot, often 40 °C in Nepalgunj, but Bardia's tiger odds stay high for those who can take the heat. From mid-May Kailash pilgrims start flying through Nepalgunj and Simikot, and the Limi Valley trek opens as snow melts on the passes.
months.tip: Book small-plane seats out of Nepalgunj early for May and June, when Rara visitors and Kailash groups fill the morning flights.

months.weather: Simikot 10 to 23 °C; Rara 8 to 20 °C, pre-monsoon showers
months.summary: June is Kailash season in Humla. Groups fly into Simikot most mornings and helicopters shuttle them to Hilsa, and the Limi Valley trek is at its best, with dry trails in the rain shadow north of the main range. Rara is still good in the first half of the month before the monsoon builds. The Terai becomes sticky and many Bardia lodges shut from late June. Khaptad hosts the Ganga Dashahara fair, which falls in late May or June.
months.tip: Keep at least one spare day in Nepalgunj in June, because cloud at Simikot can hold flights for a day or more.

months.weather: Simikot 13 to 23 °C, showers; Nepalgunj 26 to 34 °C, monsoon rain
months.summary: July is monsoon month and we do not recommend most of the region. Bardia and Shuklaphanta close to visitors or become too wet for safaris, the Karnali Highway to Jumla suffers landslides, and flights to Talcha and Jumla are often cancelled. The exception is Upper Humla, which sits partly in the rain shadow: Simikot still receives Kailash groups, and the Limi Valley is green and walkable on well-equipped camping treks. Rara is lush but hard to reach reliably.
months.tip: If you travel to Humla in July, add two spare days and carry rain gear for the lower Karnali gorge.

months.weather: Nepalgunj 26 to 33 °C, heavy rain; Simikot 12 to 22 °C
months.summary: August is still wet across the south, with flooding in the Terai and the parks mostly closed. Dhangadhi and the far-western hill districts celebrate Gaura Parva in late August or early September, with women fasting, Deuda songs and circle dances in village courtyards, the best cultural reason to visit in the monsoon. Humla remains the one trekking option, with Limi treks and Kailash pilgrims passing through Simikot whenever flights allow.
months.tip: Ask us for the exact Gaura dates each year, because they follow the lunar calendar and shift between August and September.

months.weather: Rara 7 to 18 °C, clearing late month; Simikot 9 to 21 °C
months.summary: September is a month of change. Rain eases from the middle of the month, and by the last week Rara and Jumla flights are regular again and the trails dry out. Humla is excellent, with clear skies over the Limi Valley and the last Kailash groups of the season. Gaura Parva may fall in early September. Bardia and Shuklaphanta generally reopen in late September or October, once roads and river crossings inside the parks are repaired.
months.tip: Plan Rara trips for the last ten days of September or later, when the risk of cancelled flights drops.

months.summary: October is the best all-round month. Skies are clear after the monsoon, Rara Lake is at its deepest blue, and the Jumla–Rara trek and Khaptad plateau are dry, with long views of Api, Saipal and the Kanjiroba range. Bardia reopens with green, tall grass, which makes tigers harder to spot but shows the forest at its best. Dashain and Tihar holidays bring domestic visitors to Rara, so book flights and lodges early. Limi's passes stay open until about mid-October.
months.tip: Avoid flying on the main Dashain days, when domestic seats sell out across western Nepal.

months.summary: November is clear and settled. Rara and Khaptad are cold at night, below freezing at the lake, but days are bright and the trails empty after the festival season. In the Terai, dry weather returns to Bardia and Shuklaphanta, swamp deer begin to gather on the Shuklaphanta phanta, and the tall grass starts to dry. It is a good month to combine a hill trip with a safari. Snow begins to close the high passes in Humla.
months.tip: Bring a sleeping bag rated to −10 °C for Rara in November; lodges provide only blankets.

months.weather: Bardia 8 to 24 °C, misty mornings; Jumla −6 to 12 °C
months.summary: December belongs to the Terai. Bardia and Shuklaphanta are cool and dry, with fog that clears by late morning, and lodges are quiet outside the Christmas week. Wildlife watching is good for elephants, deer and birds, including migrant waterfowl at Rani Tal and Ghodaghodi Tal, though tigers are less visible than in spring. The hills are cold and quiet: Rara and Jumla flights run less often and Khaptad sees snow.
months.tip: Combine Shuklaphanta with a stop at Ghodaghodi Tal near Dhangadhi for winter birds.

faqs.q: How do I reach Rara Lake from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Fly Kathmandu to Nepalgunj in about an hour, stay overnight, then take a morning flight of about 45 minutes to Talcha airport and walk 1.5–2 hours to the lake. Flights run a few times a week and depend on weather. Alternatives are a trek of 5–6 days from Jumla, a two-day jeep trip via Surkhet and Jumla, or a helicopter charter from Nepalgunj.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Rara Lake?
faqs.a: April to June and late September to November. Spring brings mild days of about 4–19 °C and calm water; October and November give the clearest skies and the deepest blue colour. Avoid July and August, when the monsoon cancels flights and closes the road, and December to February, when snow and frozen shores make the trip cold and unreliable.

faqs.q: How much does a Rara Lake tour cost from India?
faqs.a: Our 5-day Rara tour by flight from Kathmandu starts from about ₹62,000 or US$730 per person, twin sharing, including flights via Nepalgunj, lodges, meals at the lake and a guide. An 8-day road trip from Lucknow combining Bardia and Rara starts from about ₹68,000. A shared seat on a helicopter day tour from Nepalgunj starts from about ₹1,15,000.

faqs.q: Is Bardia good for seeing tigers?
faqs.a: Yes. Nepal's 2026 census counted 112 tigers in Bardia, and the park receives far fewer visitors than Chitwan. Guests who stay three or four nights between February and May, with a full-day jeep safari and a walking day, often see a tiger. Sightings are never guaranteed, and from October to January the tall grass makes them harder.

faqs.q: How do I go to Bardia from Lucknow?
faqs.a: Drive about 190 km to the Rupaidiha–Nepalgunj border in 4–5 hours via Bahraich, complete Nepal entry formalities, then drive about 95 km to Thakurdwara in 2.5–3 hours. Allow 6–7 hours in all. Indian citizens need a passport or voter ID card. Our Lucknow departures include the car, help at the border and park fees.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Simikot and the Limi Valley?
faqs.a: Simikot town needs no trekking permit, but the Karnali trail to Hilsa and the Limi Valley are restricted areas. You need a Humla restricted area permit, arranged through a registered agency, which has cost US$50 per person for the first week and US$10 per day after, plus a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there hotels at Rara Lake?
faqs.a: Only simple lodges and community homestays near the park office and at Talcha, with twin rooms, shared toilets, dal bhat and blankets. Building on the shore is restricted, so there is no resort or star-rated hotel. Rooms fill in April and October, so we book early and bring tents for park-approved camping when needed. Pack a warm sleeping bag.

faqs.q: Can I combine Bardia and Rara Lake in one trip?
faqs.a: Yes. Both are reached through Nepalgunj, so a week works well: two or three nights in Bardia for safaris, a night in Nepalgunj, a flight to Talcha and two nights at Rara. Our 8-day tour from Lucknow follows this route. April and early May suit both places, though Bardia is hot by then.

faqs.q: Is far west Nepal safe for tourists?
faqs.a: Yes. The far west is peaceful and people welcome visitors, including Indian families. The real risks are practical: cancelled mountain flights, landslides on hill roads in the monsoon, heat in the Terai in May, cold at Rara and Simikot, and altitude on Humla treks. Travel with spare days, insurance that covers helicopter rescue and a local guide.
